title: The blade of grass
hookLine: a single blade of grass that fire cannot burn and wind cannot lift
carry: every power is borrowed from brahman
last: WITHOUT HER, HE CANNOT EVEN STIR.

lines: FIRE CAN'T BURN IT. WIND CAN'T LIFT IT.
cards: The gods have just won a victory, and they're very pleased with themselves. So begins a short scene in the Kena Upanishad. Then something appears that they don't recognize: a mysterious being, a yaksha.
Agni, the fire, goes up to it, boasting that he can burn anything on earth. The being sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. Agni throws everything he has at it.
The grass doesn't even scorch. Then Vayu, the wind, who says he can carry off anything at all. He can't lift it an inch.
Two gods, two powers, one straw.

teach.b: Next the gods send Indra, their king.

teach.h: THE BEING VANISHES. UMA IS THERE.
teach.b: He walks toward the being, and it vanishes. In that same space he meets a woman, radiant and beautifully adorned: Uma, the daughter of the Himalaya. He asks what it was.
She answers: that was Brahman, the ultimate reality. Your victory was its victory, and you took the credit. First, the lesson about power.
Fire could burn and wind could blow because something greater let them. Take that away, and even a blade of grass is too heavy. The gods' powers were real, but borrowed.
Second, who explains it. The one who can name Brahman to the king of the gods is Uma, a woman of the mountains.

teach.h: UMA IS THE ONE WHO KNOWS.
teach.b: Later tradition knows Uma as a name of Parvati, Shiva's wife. Some who worship the goddess point to this scene: when the gods are lost, Shakti is the teacher who stands in the empty place and speaks.
Third, where she appears: in the very space where the being vanished. Some readers hear the heart of the idea there.
Brahman is beyond sight, beyond fire and wind; Shakti is the side of that reality that turns toward you, the face that answers. Fourth, the plainest.

The scene begins with pride, the ego, ahankara, saying I did this, and ends with a question. That's why so many Hindus close a prayer or a day's work by offering it back: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna.
The Upanishad says Agni, Vayu and Indra came to stand above the other gods because they came closest to Brahman, and Indra above them because he was the first to know it.

how: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Vedanta schools, and the scene of Uma explaining Brahman to Indra is retold in talks on the goddess.

games.q: what does “shakti as a philosophy” mean?
o: power as the face of Brahman that turns and answers
the pride of gods who win a battle by themselves
a contest where the strongest god wins the throne

games.q: the blade of grass — tap the pairs.
p: the being vanished as he came

s: Agni burned the blade of grass on his second try
he threw everything he had at it, and it didn't even scorch.
Uma appears in the same space where the being vanished
Indra meets her right there and asks what it was.
the gods' victory was their own doing
Uma tells them it was Brahman's victory, and they took the credit.

games.q: you're Indra, king of the gods. you walk toward the mysterious being, and it vanishes. what do you do?
o: go back and tell the gods it was nothing.
stay in that space, and ask the woman who appears there.
send Agni again with more fire.
games.why: Indra stays, meets Uma, the daughter of the Himalaya, and asks. she tells him: that was Brahman.

practice: Think of one thing that went well this week. Trace the power behind it: the breath, the teachers, the body you didn't make. Then do what many Hindus do at the end of a prayer or a task, and offer it back.
If you pray, say Krishnarpanam, or offered to you, in the name you use for God. If you don't, say quietly: not only mine.

wordCard.voice: Shakti as a philosophy. In the Kena Upanishad, fire and wind fail before one blade of grass, and Uma stands where the mystery vanished and names it Brahman.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Uma, the goddess who explains Brahman to Indra in the Kena Upanishad; a name of Parvati.

carryVoice: Your line: every power is borrowed from Brahman. Even fire burns only because Brahman lets it. See you tomorrow.
